head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: If the total is not divisible by 3, three equal parts are impossible
The sum each part must have
Sum of the part currently being built
A part is complete; start counting the next one
Cutting greedily as soon as the target is reached
At least three complete parts were found
Final check (extra parts happen when `target` is 0)

p: Three parts were found, so the result is `True`.

When the target is 0 the running sum can return to 0 many times, giving more than three cuts. Extra cuts can be merged into the last part without changing its sum (zero sums), so any count of at least 3 means the array can be split into three equal parts.

1013.takeaway: The total must be divisible by 3; then count how many times the running sum hits the target and reset, needing at least three hits.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: One dictionary per index; `dp[i][d]` is the length of the longest arithmetic subsequence that ends at `i` with common difference `d`. A missing difference counts as length 1 (just the element itself).
The state needs a difference as well as an index
Difference when `nums[j]` is the previous element
Trying every earlier element as predecessor
Extend the best chain ending at `j` with the same difference
Any two elements form an arithmetic sequence
The array has at least two elements

p: `nums = [9,4,7,2,10]`. Only the non-trivial updates are shown.
The chain 4, 7, 10 has length 3, the answer.

blocks.h: Why does overwriting `dp[i][d]` for each `j` still work?
p: If two earlier elements `j < j'` have the same value, then `dp[j'][d]` is at least `dp[j][d]` (any chain ending at `j` can instead end at `j'`). Since `j'` is processed later, the stored value ends up being the best one.

bullets: Time: O(n^2), a double loop with constant dictionary work.
Space: O(n^2), up to n differences stored per index.

1027.takeaway: For each pair (j, i) extend the longest chain ending at j that has the same difference, using a dictionary of differences per index.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Union-Find (also called Disjoint Set Union, DSU) structure over the 26 letters; each letter starts in its own group
Grouping items by an equivalence relation
Follows parent links to the group's representative, shortening the path as it goes (path compression)
Asking which group a letter belongs to
Merge two groups and keep the smaller letter as the representative
You want the minimum of each group
Replace each letter by its group's representative, which is the smallest letter in the group

p: `s1 = "parker"`, `s2 = "morris"`.
For `baseStr = "parser"`: p→m, a→a, r→k, s→k, e→e, r→k, giving `"makkek"`.

blocks.h: Why is the root always the smallest letter?
p: Every merge makes the smaller root the parent of the larger one, so a group's root can only get smaller, and the root of a group is never replaced by something bigger. After all merges, `find` returns the minimum letter of the group.

bullets: Time: O((n + m) · α(26)), effectively linear (α, the inverse Ackermann function, is tiny).

1061.takeaway: Union-Find over letters where the smaller letter always becomes the root, so find() returns each letter's smallest equivalent.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Length of the shortest string that has both `str1[i:]` and `str2[j:]` as subsequences
Suffix-based DP (dynamic programming) so we can reconstruct left to right
`i == n: dp = m - j` and `j == m: dp = n - i`
If one string is used up, the rest of the other is appended
Equal characters are shared, so only one copy is needed
Otherwise output one of the two characters and move that string forward
reconstruction `while i < n and j < m`
Walks the table from `(0, 0)` and emits characters along the cheapest path
Recovering the actual string, not just its length

p: `str1 = "abac"`, `str2 = "cab"`. The table `dp` (rows `i = 0..4`, columns `j = 0..3`) is:

Reconstruction from `(0,0)`: `a` vs `c` differ and `dp[1][0] = 5` is not `<= dp[0][1] = 4`, so emit `c` (j=1). Then `a == a`: emit `a`. Then `b == b`: emit `b`. `str2` is finished, so append `str1[2:] = "ac"`. Result: `"cabac"`, length `dp[0][0] = 5`.

blocks.h: Why `dp[i+1][j] <= dp[i][j+1]` picks the right move?
p: At a mismatch we must output one of the two characters. Emitting `str1[i]` leaves `dp[i+1][j]` characters still to place, and emitting `str2[j]` leaves `dp[i][j+1]`. Taking the smaller one keeps the total at the minimum.

bullets: Time: O(n · m) for the table and O(n + m) for the reconstruction.

1092.takeaway: Compute the shortest supersequence length for every pair of suffixes, then rebuild the string by following the cheaper move at each mismatch.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Canonical form of a domino: smaller number first, so `[1,2]` and `[2,1]` look the same
Number of dominoes of each canonical shape
Number of pairs among `c` equal dominoes
Counting unordered pairs in a group

p: Only the group of size 2 has pairs: 2·1/2 = 1.
Each of the `c` dominoes can pair with the other `c - 1`, and every pair is counted twice, once from each side.

bullets: Space: O(number of distinct dominoes), at most 45.

1128.takeaway: Normalise each domino by sorting it, count identical ones, and add C(c, 2) for each group.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: `Counter(v for row in mat for v in row)`
How many times each value appears across the whole matrix
A value that appears once per row appears exactly `len(mat)` times, because each row is strictly increasing and so has no repeats
Smallest such value, or `-1` if there is none
Min of a possibly empty sequence

p: `mat` has 4 rows. Some counts across the matrix:
Only `5` reaches 4, so the answer is `5`.

blocks.h: Why does the count work here?
p: Rows are strictly increasing, so a value can occur at most once per row. A total count equal to the number of rows therefore means it occurs in every row.

bullets: Space: O(number of distinct values), at most m · n.

1198.takeaway: Count every value across the matrix; because rows have no duplicates, a value with count equal to the number of rows is in every row.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Best path sums that end in each column of the previous row
Column indices sorted by their path sum
Columns holding the smallest and second smallest path sums
Only these two can be the best predecessor
Use the smallest previous sum unless it is in the same column, then use the second smallest
The cheapest path ending anywhere in the last row

p: The minimum of the last row is `13`.

For column `j` we need the smallest previous sum from any other column. If the global smallest sits in column `j`, the next best is the second smallest; otherwise the global smallest is allowed. So only the smallest and second smallest values matter.

bullets: Time: O(n^2 log n) because of the sort per row (O(n^2) is possible by tracking the two minima in one scan).

1289.takeaway: Row by row, each cell adds its value to the smallest previous sum in a different column, which only needs the two smallest previous sums.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Generating a sequence of length n
Values `-(n-1), -(n-3), ..., n-1`, evenly spaced and symmetric around 0

p: The values are distinct and sum to 0. For `n = 4`: `-3, -1, 1, 3`.

blocks.h: Why does the sum come out as 0?
p: The sum is `2 · (0 + 1 + ... + (n-1)) − n(n−1) = n(n−1) − n(n−1) = 0`. The values increase by 2 each step, so they are all different.

1304.takeaway: Use the symmetric sequence 2i − (n − 1): it is strictly increasing and cancels itself out.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Length of the longest word, which is how many vertical strings there are
The `c`-th character of each word, or a space if the word is too short
Remove trailing spaces only (leading ones must stay)

p: `s = "HOW ARE YOU"`, words `HOW`, `ARE`, `YOU`.
For `"TO BE OR NOT TO BE"`, column 2 has only `NOT`'s `T`, so the raw string is `"   T  "` and after `rstrip` it becomes `"   T"`, keeping its leading spaces.
The leading spaces mark where shorter words ended, so they are part of the answer. Only the spaces after the last real character are forbidden.

bullets: Space: O(words × width) for the output.

1324.takeaway: Build one string per column from the c-th letter of every word (spaces for short words) and trim trailing spaces.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Number of bits needed to write `num` in binary
Number of divide-by-2 steps: from the top bit down to 1
Shifting right until one bit is left
Number of 1 bits, each costs one "subtract 1" step
Zero needs no steps (and `bit_length() - 1` would be -1)

p: `num = 14 = 1110` in binary.
There are 3 halvings (bit length 4 minus 1) and 3 subtractions (three 1 bits), 6 steps in total.
Every 1 bit has to be cleared by a subtraction, and every bit except the highest has to be shifted out by a halving. The two kinds of steps are independent, so we just add them.

bullets: Time: O(1) for fixed-size integers (O(log n) in general).

1342.takeaway: Steps = (number of bits − 1) halvings plus (number of 1 bits) subtractions.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: A 5-bit number; bit `k` says whether vowel `k` has appeared an odd number of times so far
Flip the bit of a vowel; consonants flip nothing
The earliest index where each mask was seen; the empty prefix has mask 0 at index -1
`if mask in first: best = max(best, i - first[mask])`
Same mask at two positions means every vowel appeared an even number of times in between
Remember the first time a mask appears
Keeping the earliest index gives the longest substring

p: `s = "leetcode"`. Bits: a=1, e=2, i=4, o=8, u=16.
The longest valid substring is `"leetc"`, length 5.

blocks.h: Why do equal masks mean even counts?
p: The mask after position `i` is the parity of each vowel count in `s[0..i]`. If the parities are the same after positions `a` and `b`, the substring between them added an even amount of each vowel. Keeping the earliest index for every mask makes that substring as long as possible.

1371.takeaway: Track vowel parities as a bitmask and take the longest gap between two equal masks.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Adjacency lists of the undirected tree
Depth-first search (DFS) from vertex `u`, reached at `time` with probability `prob`
Following the frog along each root-to-leaf path
`children = [v for v in adj[u] if v != parent]`
Unvisited neighbours (in a tree, all neighbours except the one we came from)
The frog chooses uniformly among its children
Return `prob` only if the frog ends up here at time `t`, or is stuck here earlier (no children)
The frog may stay forever on a leaf
Another vertex at the end of the time or stuck: not the target
The target is in exactly one branch; return as soon as it is found

p: At vertex 4, `u == target` and `time == t`, so it returns `1/6 ≈ 0.16667`.

blocks.h: Why must the frog be stuck or out of time?
p: If the frog reaches the target before time is up and still has an unvisited neighbour, it must keep jumping, so it will not be on the target at time `t`. Only when it has no children can it stay there; otherwise the time must be exactly `t`.

bullets: Time: O(n), each vertex is visited once.
Space: O(n) for the adjacency lists and recursion stack.

1377.takeaway: DFS from vertex 1 multiplying probabilities by 1/(number of children); the target counts only if the time is exactly t or the frog has nowhere to go.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Size of each group (group key = digit sum)
`sum(1 for v in cnt.values() if v == top)`
How many groups have that size

p: `n = 13`: digit sums of 1..13.
The largest size is 2 and four groups have it, so the answer is `4`.

bullets: Time: O(n log n), each number has O(log n) digits.
Space: O(number of distinct digit sums), at most 36 for `n <= 10^4`.

1399.takeaway: Group the numbers by digit sum, find the biggest group size, and count how many groups have it.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Index of the previous 1, set so that the first 1 can never violate the rule
Number of zeros strictly between the previous 1 and this one
Remember this 1 for the next comparison

p: No violation, so the result is `True`.
If every pair of consecutive 1s is far enough apart, any two non-consecutive 1s are even farther apart. So checking neighbours is enough.

1437.takeaway: Scan once, remember the last 1, and check that the zeros between consecutive 1s number at least k.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The two largest values, in ascending order

p: All values are at least 1, so `x − 1` is non-negative and increases with `x`. A product of two non-negative numbers is largest when both numbers are as large as possible.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) because of the sort (a single pass tracking the two largest gives O(n)).
Space: O(n) for the sorted copy.

1464.takeaway: Take the two largest numbers and multiply their values minus one.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: How many numbers have each remainder mod `k` (Python's `%` is never negative, so negative numbers are handled)
Remainder 0 numbers must pair with each other, so their count must be even
Remainder exactly `k/2` also pairs with itself, so its count must be even
Remainders `r` and `k − r` add up to `k`, so they must be present equally often

p: All checks pass, so the result is `True`.

Two numbers sum to a multiple of `k` exactly when their remainders add to 0 or `k`. So every number with remainder `r` needs a partner with remainder `k − r`, and the pairing exists exactly when the two counts match (or each self-pairing count is even).

1497.takeaway: Count remainders mod k and check that r and k − r occur equally often (and 0 and k/2 occur an even number of times).

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Every subarray sum is produced by extending the right end one element at a time
Generating all subarray sums in O(1) each
Put the sums in non-decreasing order
The question refers to the sorted order

p: With `n <= 1000` there are about 500,000 subarray sums, which is small enough to build and sort directly. A heap or binary search is only needed for much larger inputs.

bullets: Time: O(n^2 log n) for building and sorting about n²/2 sums.

1508.takeaway: Generate all subarray sums, sort them, and sum the slice from left to right.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Number of odd integers in `[0, high]`
Counting odd numbers up to a bound
Number of odd integers in `[0, low − 1]`
Counting in a range as a difference of prefix counts

p: `low = 3`, `high = 7`.

blocks.h: Why does `(x + 1) // 2` count odds up to x?
p: Among 0 to x there is one odd number for every two integers, with the odd one coming second in each pair (1, 3, 5, ...). Rounding up with `(x + 1) // 2` handles both parities of x.

1523.takeaway: Count odds up to high minus odds below low with the O(1) formula (x + 1) // 2.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Number of trailing zeros of each row
A row only matters through how far its zeros extend from the right
Row `i` must end with at least `n − 1 − i` zeros so that everything above the diagonal is 0
Find the nearest row at or below `i` that has enough zeros
Greedy: take the closest suitable row
Moving that row up to position `i` takes `j − i` adjacent swaps
Cost of bringing a row up
Simulate the move by taking the row out and inserting it at `i`
No row below can satisfy the requirement

p: Total swaps = 3.

blocks.h: Why is the greedy choice right?
p: Positions are filled from the top, and the top positions have the strictest needs. Choosing the nearest row that meets the need costs the fewest swaps, and moving it up only shifts the rows in between down by one, which does not hurt them. Rows with more zeros than needed can serve later positions, so nothing is wasted.

1536.takeaway: Reduce each row to its trailing-zero count, then fill positions top-down with the nearest row that has enough zeros.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: All boundary points of the stick, including both ends
Turning the problem into one over segments
Minimum cost to fully cut the part of the stick from `pos[i]` to `pos[j]` (using only the cuts strictly between them)
Cost of the first cut on this piece: its whole length
The cost depends on the piece length
`min(dp[i][k] + dp[k][j] for k in range(i + 1, j))`
Choose which cut `k` happens first; the two halves are then independent
Splitting an interval at its first (or last) operation
Fill shorter intervals first so the pieces are ready

p: `dp[0][5] = 16`: cut at 3 first (cost 7), then the left piece `[0,3]` costs `dp[0][2] = 3` and the right piece `[3,7]` costs `dp[2][5] = 6`, which together make 9.

blocks.h: Why think of the cut as the first one?
p: After the first cut at `k`, the two resulting sticks are independent: cuts in one do not affect the other's cost. The first cut costs the full piece length, and the rest of the cost splits into two smaller instances of the same problem.

bullets: Time: O(c^3), where `c` is the number of cuts.

1547.takeaway: Interval DP over the sorted cut points: for each piece, try each cut as the first and add the piece length to the cost of the two halves.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: With an odd size, the centre cell is on both diagonals and was added twice, so subtract it once

p: Centre cell is `5`, so the result is `30 − 5 = 25`.
The two diagonals cross at a single cell only when the size is odd. For an even size they never share a cell, so nothing is double counted.

1572.takeaway: Add both diagonals row by row and subtract the centre cell once when the size is odd.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Extends `j` over a run of balloons with the same colour
Total removal time of the run and the most expensive balloon in it
Within a run keep the costliest balloon and remove all the others
Greedy: keep the one that is costly to remove
Jump to the start of the next run

p: `colors = "abaac"`, `neededTime = [1,2,3,4,5]`.
The answer is `3`: remove the balloon with time 3.

blocks.h: Why does each run reduce to one balloon?
p: Within a run of equal colours, adjacent balloons clash, so all but one must go. To pay the least, keep the one with the highest removal time. Different runs do not interact, because the balloons between them already have different colours at the boundary.

1578.takeaway: For each run of equal colours, remove everything except the most expensive balloon.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Splitting on any amount of whitespace
With one word there are no gaps, so every space goes to the end
Spaces in each gap and the leftover
Join words with equal gaps, then put the leftover at the end

p: `text = "  this   is  a sentence "`.

head: Quantity
Value
rows: this, is, a, sentence (4 words, so 3 gaps)

p: `len(words) - 1` would be zero and `divmod` would fail. With a single word there is nowhere to put spaces except after it.

1592.takeaway: Count spaces and words, split spaces evenly across the gaps, and put the remainder at the end.
